subsection: 1. The Home Rule Bill, World War I and the 1916 Rising, 1912–1916

notes.b: Home Rule was the Liberal government's policy for Ireland. Its passage depended on the Irish Parliamentary Party and on the new limits the Parliament Act 1911 had placed on the House of Lords.
points: Asquith's Liberal government introduced the Third Home Rule Bill in April 1912.
The Bill proposed an Irish parliament in Dublin with control of most domestic affairs; Westminster kept reserved matters such as the Crown, defence, foreign policy and customs.
The Parliament Act 1911 reduced the Lords' power to a delaying veto, so a bill passed by the Commons three times over about two years could become law without Lords' consent.
The Lords rejected the Bill in 1913 and again in 1914, so it went back to the Commons; it passed its third Commons reading in May 1914.
The Government of Ireland Act received royal assent on 18 September 1914, but a Suspensory Act postponed its operation until after the war.
A Buckingham Palace Conference in July 1914 failed to agree how Ulster counties could be excluded from Home Rule.
An Amending Bill to provide a temporary exclusion for Ulster was promised in 1914 but never passed into law.
Under the Act's terms Ireland would keep 42 MPs at Westminster, a reduction from the 103 Irish seats of the time.

notes.b: Unionist opposition to Home Rule took the form of mass protest and then armed organisation, and nationalists answered by forming their own volunteers.
points: On Ulster Day, 28 September 1912, about 470,000 men signed the Ulster Covenant pledging to resist Home Rule; Edward Carson and James Craig led the campaign.
The Ulster Volunteer Force was formed in January 1913 to resist Home Rule by force if necessary.
The Irish Volunteers were founded in Dublin in November 1913 in response to the UVF, with Eoin MacNeill as their public leader.
The UVF landed a large consignment of rifles at Larne, Co. Antrim, in April 1914.
The Irish Volunteers landed German rifles at Howth, Co. Dublin, on 26 July 1914, using Erskine Childers's yacht Asgard.
On the same day, 26 July 1914, British soldiers fired on a jeering crowd at Bachelor's Walk in Dublin, killing three civilians.

In June 1914 John Redmond's supporters gained control of the Volunteer committee, and in September 1914 most members followed Redmond into the National Volunteers, leaving a smaller Irish Volunteers group under MacNeill.

notes.h: World War I and the Home Rule settlement, 1914–1916
notes.b: The outbreak of war in August 1914 changed the Home Rule question: the Bill was suspended, and nationalist leaders and Volunteers were pulled into the British war effort.
points: On 20 September 1914 at Woodenbridge, Co. Wicklow, John Redmond urged the Volunteers to serve wherever they were needed, including in the British army, to win Home Rule.
The 10th (Irish) Division fought at Suvla Bay in the Gallipoli campaign in August 1915.
The 16th (Irish) Division fought on the Somme in 1916, including at Guillemont and Ginchy in September.
The 36th (Ulster) Division attacked near Thiepval on the first day of the Somme, 1 July 1916, and suffered heavy losses.
Irish farmers and food producers gained from wartime demand and high prices, but the war also brought shortages and rising costs for urban workers.
Redmond's party lost influence as the war dragged on: the Irish Parliamentary Party had no power to deliver Home Rule while the Bill was suspended.
Redmond died in March 1918, before the conscription crisis and the general election that ended the Parliamentary Party's dominance.

notes.h: The IRB Military Council and the planning of the Rising, 1914–1916
notes.b: The Rising was planned by a small group within the Irish Republican Brotherhood and carried out with the Irish Citizen Army. Its plans depended on German help that never fully arrived.
points: The IRB's Military Council, led by Tom Clarke and including Patrick Pearse and Seán MacDiarmada, planned an armed rising in 1915 and 1916.
Roger Casement went to Germany in 1914 to seek German support, including arms and an Irish brigade formed from prisoners of war.
The Aud, a German ship carrying arms for the Rising, was intercepted and scuttled off Cork Harbour on 21 April 1916.
Casement landed by German submarine on Good Friday, 21 April 1916, at Banna Strand, Co. Kerry, and was arrested soon after.
On 23 April 1916 MacNeill published a countermand of Volunteer manoeuvres, cancelling the planned rising for that Sunday.
After the countermand the Military Council postponed the rising by a day and went ahead on Easter Monday, 24 April, with only part of the Volunteers.
James Connolly brought the Irish Citizen Army into the planning; it was a socialist armed force formed in 1913 during the Dublin Lockout.

notes.b: The Rising lasted six days in Dublin and was defeated militarily, but its occupation of the city centre and its proclamation of a republic made it a turning point.
points: On Easter Monday, 24 April 1916, Volunteers and the Citizen Army seized the General Post Office on O'Connell Street as their headquarters.

Pearse read the Proclamation of the Irish Republic from the steps of the GPO; it was signed by Pearse, Tom Clarke, Seán MacDiarmada, Thomas MacDonagh, Joseph Plunkett, Éamonn Ceannt and James Connolly.

Garrisons were set up at Boland's Mill (under de Valera), the South Dublin Union (Ceannt), Jacob's factory (MacDonagh), St Stephen's Green and the College of Surgeons (Michael Mallin, with Markievicz), and the Four Courts (Edward Daly).
Seán Connolly, one of the Citizen Army leaders, was the first rebel killed, shot in an attack on Dublin Castle on the first day.
Dublin Castle and the main British military barracks were not captured, and reinforcements from Britain and the Curragh restored British control over the city centre.
Fighting destroyed much of O'Connell Street and central Dublin by fire and shelling; the GPO was abandoned on 29 April.
Pearse ordered a surrender on Saturday 29 April 1916; about 485 people died in the week, with civilians the largest group, and several thousand were wounded (figures vary between sources).
Martial law was declared in Dublin on 24 April, and British authorities took control of the city.

notes.h: The executions and the shift in opinion, May–August 1916
notes.b: The British response turned a military defeat into a political crisis. The executions changed public opinion and made the Rising a source of nationalist legitimacy.
points: Courts-martial sentenced rebel leaders to death, and fifteen men were shot by firing squad at Kilmainham Gaol between 3 and 12 May 1916.
Pearse, Tom Clarke and Thomas MacDonagh were among the first executed on 3 May.
James Connolly, badly wounded in the Rising, was shot while seated in a chair on 12 May; he was the last to be executed.
Thousands were arrested after the Rising, and many were held without trial in internment camps in England and Wales, including Frongoch in north Wales.
Augustine Birrell resigned as Chief Secretary for Ireland in May 1916; Asquith visited Dublin and the government sent General Sir John Maxwell to command.
Lloyd George's attempt at a settlement in June and July 1916, which proposed temporary exclusion of the six counties, failed.
Roger Casement was tried for treason in London and hanged at Pentonville Prison on 3 August 1916.
Opinion shifted from hostility, in which many Dubliners had jeered the rebels as they were marched away, to sympathy, and Sinn Féin gained support as the Parliamentary Party lost ground.

notes.b: Pearse was the Rising's most prominent leader and its chief ideologue. He is judged both as an educator and as an advocate of violent sacrifice.
points: Pearse (1879–1916) was a teacher, writer and Gaelic League figure who edited the League's newspaper, An Claidheamh Soluis, from 1903.
He founded St Enda's school in Dublin in 1908, teaching through Irish and combining Irish culture with a practical education.
In 1913 he joined the Irish Republican Brotherhood, and he became prominent in the Irish Volunteers, serving as their commandant-general.
At the funeral of Fenian leader O'Donovan Rossa on 1 August 1915 he spoke of the Fenian dead; his words, ‘the fools, the fools, the fools’, were aimed at British policy towards Ireland.
He was a leader of the Military Council and the President of the Provisional Government proclaimed during the Rising.
He read the Proclamation at the GPO, commanded the rebel forces in Dublin, and ordered the surrender on 29 April 1916.
Pearse was executed by firing squad at Kilmainham Gaol on 3 May 1916, aged 36.
Contemporaries split: Dublin crowds and the Parliamentary Party condemned the Rising at first, while the executions later made him a martyr.
Historians have judged him on his idealism and educational work, and on his writings that praised ‘blood sacrifice’; critics such as Conor Cruise O'Brien condemned that strand of his thought.

notes.b: Markievicz was a participant in the Rising and a witness to its aftermath. This part of her career covers her role up to 1916; her later career is in the notes on the second Sinn Féin.
points: Constance Gore-Booth (1868–1927) was born into a Sligo Anglo-Irish family, trained as a painter in Paris, and married the Polish count Casimir Markievicz in 1900.
She was active in Inghinidhe na hÉireann and in the cultural nationalist movement before she joined the Irish Citizen Army in 1913.
During the Rising she was second-in-command of the Citizen Army garrison at St Stephen's Green and the College of Surgeons.
After the surrender she was court-martialled and sentenced to death; the sentence was commuted to life imprisonment because she was a woman.
She was released under a general amnesty in June 1917 and was later the first woman elected to the House of Commons in 1918, though she did not take her seat.
Contemporaries saw her as a dramatic figure whose gender made her sentence and release stand out; later historians emphasise her commitment to the Irish Citizen Army and to labour and women's causes.

notes.h: Assessment: the Rising's achievements and limits
notes.b: Judgements on the Rising depend on whether success is measured by military outcome, by the Proclamation's aims, or by its long-term political effect.
points: Militarily the Rising failed: it was contained within a week, the leaders were executed, and the rebels had little popular backing in the first days.
Politically it succeeded: the executions and the Proclamation's republican aims turned the Rising into a source of legitimacy for Sinn Féin.
Contemporary unionists and the Irish Parliamentary Party condemned the rebels as wasteful and reckless; nationalist opinion came to see the executions as a British error.
Later historians debate how far the Rising had popular support before the executions, with revisionists stressing limited popular backing and others stressing its ideals and the reaction it provoked.
Yeats's line ‘A terrible beauty is born’, from his poem Easter 1916, captures the view that the Rising changed Irish politics in ways its leaders could not control.
The Home Rule Bill's suspension meant Redmond's constitutional policy lost ground, and the Home Rule settlement was overtaken by partition in the 1920 Government of Ireland Act.
Commemoration of the Rising in 1966, the fiftieth anniversary, showed how the event had become central to the national story.

keyTerms.definition: The 1912 bill to give Ireland a devolved parliament in Dublin within the United Kingdom, passed by the Commons in 1914 and suspended for the duration of the war.
The armed unionist force formed in January 1913 to resist Home Rule, which imported rifles at Larne in April 1914.
The nationalist armed force founded in November 1913 as a response to the UVF, which split in 1914 when most members followed Redmond.
The use of armed violence to achieve political ends, a tradition that Pearse and the IRB argued was necessary to win independence.
The Irish Republican Brotherhood was the secret oath-bound society that planned the 1916 Rising; the Irish Republican Army was the name adopted by the Volunteers from 1919.
Pearse's belief that the willing death of nationalists in armed struggle would regenerate the nation and win Irish freedom.
The small IRB group that planned the 1916 Rising and took the key military decisions in the weeks before it.
The document read by Pearse at the GPO on 24 April 1916, declaring an Irish Republic and a provisional government.
The Act that reduced the House of Lords' power to a two-year delaying veto over bills passed by the Commons, making Home Rule possible.
The Home Rule Act that received royal assent in September 1914 but was suspended until the end of the war.
The socialist armed force formed by James Connolly and Jack White in 1913 during the Dublin Lockout, which fought alongside the Volunteers in 1916.
